findings.title: Service layer does not handle KeyError from TicketStore.get
findings.explanation: TicketStore.get was changed to raise KeyError when a ticket is missing. The service layer's get method still checks for a None return value and raises TicketNotFound, so a missing ticket now propagates a KeyError instead of the intended TicketNotFound, breaking callers and tests that expect TicketNotFound.
findings.verification_note: Service layer still checks for a None return (if ticket is None: raise TicketNotFound) but TicketStore.get now raises KeyError, so the exception propagates instead of being converted to TicketNotFound.

findings.title: KeyError may expose ticket IDs and cause unhandled exception
findings.explanation: TicketStore.get now raises KeyError(ticket_id) when a ticket is missing; callers (e.g., tickets/service.py) expect a None return and raise a custom TicketNotFound, so the KeyError can propagate to higher layers, potentially leaking the internal ticket ID and causing an unhandled exception that may reveal stack traces or cause denial‑of‑service.

evidence.quote:
if ticket is None:
    raise TicketNotFound(ticket_id)

findings.verification_note: TicketStore.get raises KeyError(ticket_id) and callers (e.g., tickets/service.py) do not catch it, allowing the ID to be included in an unhandled exception that could be exposed.

limitations: The surrounding application code that handles exceptions from TicketStore.get is not provided, so the exact impact (whether the KeyError is caught and transformed or results in an HTTP 500) cannot be fully determined.
